newsitem.title: NORWAY: Nobel peace award wins praise outside indonesia.
newsitem.headline: Nobel peace award wins praise outside indonesia.

text.p: The awarding of the Nobel Peace Prize to Catholic Bishop Carlos Belo of East Timor and Timorese independence activist Jose Ramos-Horta on Friday drew chilly reaction from Indonesia but warm praise abroad.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee cited the two men for their efforts to bring peace in the territory of East Timor, which Indonesia invaded and annexed after Portuguese colonisers left in 1975.

Indonesia called the award surprising. "It is the right of the committee with its own criteria to award the Nobel Peace Prize. However, we regret that a political opportunist has received the prize," Foreign Ministry spokesman Ghaffar Fadyl told Reuters in Jakarta, referring to Ramos-Horta.
"We do not know the basis on which they have given the prize," Fadyl said, declining to comment on Belo's award.

"It is quite a surprise and quite regrettable that such a reputable institution has decided to give this prize to a person like Ramos-Horta, who has quite clearly been involved in the manipulation of the people of East Timor for his own interests," he added.

In Lisbon, Portuguese political leaders were delighted, saying it could strengthen their country's hand in long-running talks on the territory's future with Indonesia, whose rule in East Timor has never been recognised by the United Nations.

"I am very pleased by the news. It is a wonderful surprise," President Joao Sampaio said. "The award reflects their indefatigable work in the service of human rights and peace in the territory," he told reporters.

The award was sweet satisfaction for Pope John Paul, who for years has supported the aspirations of the Timorese people. Because of East Timor's Portuguese colonial past, the Roman Catholic Church is the most powerful institution there after the army of predominantly Moslem Indonesia.

"It is a recognition of (Belo's) activity as a man of the Church, marked by his indefatigable search for dialogue that is always inspired by peaceful solutions," Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said. "I hope that this will help speed up the achievement of concrete results, in respect for the rights of peoples," he added.

The Australian government lauded Ramos-Horta and Bishop Belo. "We congratulate the Nobel laureates with whom we share the desire for a peaceful East Timor," a spokesman for Australian Foreign Affairs Minister Alexander Downer said.

Rory Mungoven, programme director in Asia for human rights group Amnesty International, told Reuters Television: "It really brings the problems of East Timor back into the international spotlight, not just political questions but the human rights violations that are a daily reality on the ground there."
But he suggested that any reaction to the award in East Timor might trigger a new clampdown by Indonesia.
In Rome, Mario Marazziti, spokesman for the Sant'Egidio Community, a Roman Catholic peace group involved in efforts to resolve the conflict in East Timor, expressed delight.

"I hope that the award will help create the sort of international climate which will encourage the interested parties, Portugal, Indonesia and the people of East Timor, to overcome the difficulties that still stand in the way of an agreement on reasonable settlement that respects the rights of everyone," Marazziti, who knows both men, said.

In London, Lord Avebury, chairman of the British parliamentary human rights group, said the award "ought to put the issue back on the agenda of the world community. I'm afraid in the European Union the running has been left to Portugal".
